title: Manias and Mass Behavior
description: Dancing plagues, laughter epidemics, tulip bubbles and a radio panic, and how much of each really happened

concepts.title: The Strasbourg Dancing Plague of 1518
concepts.contentHtml:
In July 1518 a woman recorded as Frau Troffea began dancing in a street in Strasbourg, then a free city of the Holy Roman Empire, and kept going for days. Within weeks others had joined her; chronicles put the number of dancers that summer anywhere from about 50 to 400. City council orders, local chronicles and later comments by the physician Paracelsus all survive, so the episode is better documented than most such marvels.

The council's first response followed the medical logic of the day. Physicians blamed overheated blood, so the afflicted were to dance it out, and the council opened guildhalls, hired musicians and paid strong men to hold the dancers up. When numbers grew, it reversed course, banned public music and dancing, and sent the dancers to a shrine of Saint Vitus near Saverne, where priests performed rituals with crosses, holy water and red shoes. By early September the outbreak had faded.

The historian John Waller, in A Time to Dance, a Time to Die (2008), reads the episode as mass psychogenic illness. Alsace had endured years of harvest failure, famine and disease, and many people believed Saint Vitus could punish sinners with compulsive dancing. Waller rejects the older theory of ergot poisoning from moldy rye, because ergotism causes convulsions and cuts off blood flow, which makes days of dancing unlikely. It also can't explain why dancing epidemics clustered along the Rhine and Moselle, as in the great outbreak of 1374.

Popular retellings often claim fifteen deaths a day. That figure is unproven, since it comes from later accounts and the Strasbourg records of 1518 don't clearly mention any deaths.

concepts.title: Laughter in Tanganyika, and a Panic That Mostly Wasn't
concepts.contentHtml:
On 30 January 1962, weeks after Tanganyika's independence, three pupils at a mission boarding school for girls in Kashasha, near the western shore of Lake Victoria, began laughing uncontrollably. Attacks of laughing and crying, with restlessness and sometimes fainting, spread to 95 of the school's 159 pupils but not to the teachers. The school closed on 18 March. Cases followed in nearby villages and schools, and reported totals reach about 1,000 people and more than a dozen school closures. Tests found no infection or toxin. The main source is a 1963 paper by Rankin and Philip in the Central African Journal of Medicine.

Researchers classify it as mass psychogenic illness, meaning genuine physical symptoms that spread through a close group under stress without an organic cause. The pattern fits: it began among adolescents in a strict institution and followed social ties. The proposed stresses, such as political change and school discipline, are interpretations rather than proven causes.

The American radio panic of 30 October 1938 is a warning about such labels. Orson Welles's Mercury Theatre on the Air presented H. G. Wells's The War of the Worlds as a run of fake news bulletins on CBS. Next morning newspapers reported stampedes and nationwide hysteria. But a C. E. Hooper ratings survey that night found only about 2 percent of respondents listening to the play, and most were tuned to a rival comedy show. Hadley Cantril's 1940 study estimated over a million frightened listeners, but scholars such as W. Joseph Campbell, Jefferson Pooley and Michael Socolow argue that newspapers, losing advertising to radio, inflated scattered alarm into legend. Some listeners were genuinely scared, but there wasn't a mass flight.

concepts.title: Tulip Mania: Smaller Than the Legend
concepts.contentHtml:
In the winter of 1636 to 1637, prices for rare tulip bulbs in the Dutch Republic rose steeply, then collapsed in early February 1637. Tradition places the first sign at an auction in Haarlem where buyers failed to bid. The prized striped and flamed tulips owed their patterns to a virus, now called tulip breaking virus, which also weakened the bulbs and kept them scarce. Much of the winter trade used contracts for future delivery, often agreed in taverns, so bulbs rarely changed hands at the peak.

You may know the popular version, which comes chiefly from Charles Mackay's Extraordinary Popular Delusions and the Madness of Crowds (1841): a whole nation gripped by speculation, ruined traders drowning themselves in canals, and a sailor jailed for eating a priceless bulb he took for an onion. Mackay leaned on earlier writers, who drew on moralizing pamphlets printed around the crash to warn against greed rather than to record facts.

Anne Goldgar's Tulipmania (2007) went to the archives, reading notarial records, court cases and wills from Haarlem and other cities. She found a fairly small circle of merchants and skilled artisans doing the trading, not the whole population. She identified only a handful of people in financial trouble in those years and couldn't show that tulips caused it. Because most contracts were never paid in full, the crash produced lawsuits and damaged trust rather than ruin, and towns let buyers cancel deals for a fraction of the price. The economist Peter Garber has argued that prices for rare bulbs followed normal patterns for novelty goods.

title: Very Odd Wars
description: Emus, a pig, a 40-minute bombardment, an ear and a football match, and the real causes behind each

concepts.title: The Great Emu War of 1932
concepts.contentHtml:
After the First World War, Western Australia settled many former soldiers on wheat farms in marginal country. By 1932 the Depression had driven wheat prices down, and after the breeding season an estimated 20,000 emus moved into farming districts around Campion and Walgoolan, eating and trampling crops and breaking fences that then let rabbits in.

The farmers, many of them veterans, asked for machine guns. The defense minister, Sir George Pearce, sent Major G. P. W. Meredith of the Royal Australian Artillery with two soldiers, two Lewis guns and 10,000 rounds. Shooting began on 2 November 1932. The emus split into small groups when fired on and outran trucks over rough ground, and at one ambush a gun jammed after only a few birds fell. Critical press coverage led to a withdrawal on 8 November. After further appeals from farmers the operation resumed around 13 November and ended on 10 December.

Meredith reported 986 kills with 9,860 rounds, exactly ten rounds per bird, plus 2,500 wounded birds he believed had died. Historians treat such tidy totals with suspicion. He praised the birds' ability to absorb bullets, comparing them to tanks. Later requests for troops were refused, and a bounty system that paid farmers to kill emus proved far more effective, with tens of thousands of bounties claimed in the following years. The name "Emu War" came from the newspapers, and the episode survives as a rare case of an army publicly bested by birds.

concepts.title: The Pig War and the Shortest War
concepts.contentHtml:
The 1846 Oregon Treaty ran the boundary between the United States and British North America along the 49th parallel and then through "the middle of the channel" separating the mainland from Vancouver Island. Two channels qualified, with the San Juan Islands between them, and both sides claimed the islands. On 15 June 1859 the American settler Lyman Cutlar shot a pig rooting in his potato patch on San Juan Island. It belonged to the Hudson's Bay Company farm run by Charles Griffin. Cutlar offered $10; Griffin wanted $100; British officials threatened arrest.

The US Army landed Captain George Pickett with 66 soldiers. By August about 461 Americans with 14 cannon faced British warships carrying some 2,140 men and 70 guns. Rear Admiral Robert Baynes refused to land troops, saying he would not involve two great nations in a war over a squabble about a pig. A joint military occupation followed until a commission appointed by the German emperor Wilhelm I awarded the islands to the United States in 1872. The pig was the only casualty.

The Anglo-Zanzibar War of 1896 was short but not harmless. When Sultan Hamad bin Thuwaini died suddenly on 25 August, his cousin Khalid bin Barghash seized the palace without the British consul's approval, which an 1890 agreement required. Britain's ultimatum expired at 9:00 am on 27 August; Royal Navy ships opened fire at 9:02, and the shooting stopped roughly 38 to 45 minutes later, depending on the source. About 500 people on the sultan's side were killed or wounded, many in the burning palace, against one seriously wounded British sailor. Khalid escaped to the German consulate.

concepts.title: Ears and Football: Names That Hide the Causes
concepts.contentHtml:
In April 1731 a Spanish coast guard ship searching for contraband stopped the British brig Rebecca in the Caribbean, and its commander, Julio León Fandiño, cut off captain Robert Jenkins's ear. In 1738 Jenkins was called before the House of Commons; the claim that he brandished the preserved ear there is often repeated but poorly documented. The name "War of Jenkins' Ear" came much later, from the historian Thomas Carlyle in 1858.

The ear was a pretext. British merchants resented Spanish limits on trade with Spain's American colonies, Spanish patrols seized British ships suspected of smuggling, and opposition politicians used these "depredations" against Robert Walpole's peace policy. Britain declared war in October 1739. Admiral Edward Vernon took Porto Bello that year, but a great expedition against Cartagena de Indias failed in 1741, with far more men lost to disease than to fighting. The war merged into the War of the Austrian Succession, which ended in 1748.

The 1969 "Football War" between El Salvador and Honduras follows the same pattern. Three World Cup qualifiers in June 1969 brought riots and attacks on fans, and El Salvador broke off diplomatic relations on 26 June, the eve of the deciding match in Mexico City. Fighting began on 14 July and lasted about 100 hours, until an Organization of American States ceasefire. The deeper causes were land and migration. More than 300,000 Salvadorans, from a small and crowded country, lived in Honduras, many farming land without title, and a Honduran land reform law of 1962, enforced from 1967, took that land and drove many out. Official death tolls were in the low hundreds; other estimates run to several thousand, mostly civilians.

title: Unlikely Disasters
description: Floods of beer and molasses, a stinking river, a lost summer and a solar storm

concepts.title: Floods of Beer and Molasses
concepts.contentHtml:
On 17 October 1814 an iron hoop failed on a 22-foot (6.7 m) vat of maturing porter at Meux and Company's Horse Shoe Brewery, near Tottenham Court Road in London. The vat burst and broke others, releasing an estimated 580,000 to 1.47 million liters of beer, which smashed a brewery wall and poured into the crowded slum of St Giles. Eight people died, all women and children, five of them mourners at a wake for a two-year-old boy. The inquest ruled the deaths accidental, and the brewery paid no compensation but later recovered the excise duty on the lost beer. Tales of crowds drinking from the gutters and of a death from alcohol poisoning are absent from contemporary newspapers, which described an orderly crowd.

On 15 January 1919 a steel tank about 50 feet (15 m) tall in Boston's North End split open, releasing some 2.3 million US gallons (8.7 million liters) of molasses. A wave estimated at up to 25 feet (8 m) high and moving at about 35 miles per hour (56 km/h) crushed buildings and buckled an elevated railway; 21 people died and about 150 were injured. A 2016 study found that the molasses thickened fast in the cold air, trapping victims and slowing rescue.

The tank, owned by United States Industrial Alcohol and holding molasses for fermentation, had leaked since its first filling in 1915; it was painted brown to hide the seepage, and it had never been properly tested. The company blamed anarchist bombers, but a court-appointed auditor, Hugh Ogden, found it responsible after three years of hearings, and it paid about $628,000 in damages. Massachusetts then tightened rules requiring licensed architects and engineers to approve such structures.

concepts.title: The Great Stink and Bazalgette's Sewers
concepts.contentHtml:
By the 1850s the spread of flush toilets was sending ever more sewage through cesspits and old drains into the Thames, the same river from which several water companies drew drinking water. In the hot summer of 1858 the smell became overpowering. Parliament hung curtains soaked in chloride of lime at the windows, and Benjamin Disraeli called the river "a Stygian pool, reeking with ineffable and intolerable horrors".

Most experts then accepted the miasma theory, which held that disease spread through foul air. That mistaken theory supplied the urgency: if the smell caused cholera, legislators were at risk at their desks. A bill became law on 2 August 1858, giving the Metropolitan Board of Works the power and money to act. Its chief engineer, Joseph Bazalgette, built about 82 miles (132 km) of large intercepting sewers running parallel to the river, fed by some 1,100 miles (1,800 km) of street sewers and using about 318 million bricks. Pumping stations such as Crossness and Abbey Mills moved the flow to outfalls downstream of the city, and the Victoria, Albert and Chelsea Embankments were built partly to carry sewers. Major sections opened in 1865, and the system was largely complete by 1875.

The sewers worked even though the theory behind them did not. Cholera is waterborne, as John Snow had argued after the Broad Street outbreak of 1854, and moving sewage away from water intakes cut deaths whatever the reason. A test came in 1866, when cholera killed more than 5,500 Londoners, mostly in an East End district not yet connected to the new system and supplied with contaminated water. Bazalgette reportedly doubled his calculated pipe sizes to allow for growth, which kept the network useful for generations.

concepts.title: 1816 and 1859: Strange Skies
concepts.contentHtml:
In April 1815 Mount Tambora on Sumbawa, in present-day Indonesia, produced the largest eruption in recorded history. Around 10,000 people died directly, and many more died of famine and disease on Sumbawa and Lombok; estimates of the total vary widely, from roughly 60,000 to 100,000 or more. Sulfate aerosols in the stratosphere cooled the globe by roughly 0.4 to 0.7 °C.

The next year, 1816, became the "Year Without a Summer". Snow fell in parts of New England and New York in June, frosts hit in July and August, crops failed across Europe, food riots broke out, and typhus spread in Ireland. Thousands of families left New England for the West. Incessant rain kept Lord Byron, Percy Shelley, Mary Godwin (later Mary Shelley) and John Polidori indoors at the Villa Diodati near Geneva in June 1816, where Byron's ghost-story challenge led to Frankenstein (1818) and Polidori's The Vampyre (1819). Suggested links to Turner's glowing sunsets and Karl Drais's 1817 running machine are plausible but unproven.

On 1 September 1859 the astronomers Richard Carrington and Richard Hodgson independently saw a brilliant white-light flare on the Sun. About 17.6 hours later a coronal mass ejection struck Earth, causing the most intense geomagnetic storm on record. Auroras appeared as far south as Cuba, Hawaii and Colombia. Telegraph systems failed across Europe and North America; operators reported sparks and shocks, and on a Boston to Portland line operators disconnected their batteries and kept working for about two hours on the induced current alone. A storm of that size today could damage power grids and satellites, which is why it now serves as a planning benchmark.

title: Remarkable Individuals
description: A self-made emperor, a pirate commander, two soldiers out of time and a famous patient whose story grew

concepts.title: Unlikely Sovereigns: Emperor Norton and Zheng Yi Sao
concepts.contentHtml:
Joshua Norton, born in England around 1818 and raised in South Africa, prospered as a San Francisco merchant until a failed attempt to corner the rice market in 1852, and the lawsuits that followed, left him bankrupt by 1856. On 17 September 1859 he delivered a proclamation to the Daily Evening Bulletin declaring himself "Emperor of these United States", and the paper printed it. Norton I went on to decree the abolition of Congress, call for a bridge or tunnel across San Francisco Bay, and issue his own scrip, which some businesses accepted. When an officer arrested him for commitment in 1867, the police chief freed him with an apology. About 10,000 people viewed his body after his death in January 1880. Some of the legend is later invention: newspapers printed fake decrees in his name, the ban on the word "Frisco" cannot be traced before 1939, and the famous dogs Bummer and Lazarus were not his.

Zheng Yi Sao, "wife of Zheng Yi" (c. 1775 to 1844), was a Cantonese woman of modest origins; the story that she worked in a floating brothel is unproven. She married the pirate Zheng Yi in 1801, and when he died in 1807 she took over his Red Flag Fleet and, with his adopted son Zhang Bao, held together a confederation estimated at tens of thousands of pirates. Its fleets defeated Qing squadrons and taxed coastal shipping. In 1810 she negotiated a surrender to the governor-general Bai Ling that pardoned most of her followers and gave Zhang Bao an official post. She later ran a gambling house in Guangzhou. The strict pirate code often credited to her was attributed by the Qing official Yuan Yonglun to Zhang Bao.

concepts.title: Soldiers Out of Time: Hiroo Onoda and Jack Churchill
concepts.contentHtml:
Hiroo Onoda, a Japanese army intelligence officer, reached Lubang Island in the Philippines in December 1944 with orders never to surrender or take his own life. With three comrades he waged a guerrilla campaign in the hills for decades, dismissing leaflets announcing Japan's surrender in 1945, and later newspapers, as enemy tricks. One comrade surrendered in 1950; the other two were killed in clashes in 1954 and 1972. In February 1974 a young Japanese traveler, Norio Suzuki, found Onoda, who would yield only to a superior's order. On 9 March his former commander, Major Yoshimi Taniguchi, by then a bookseller, read him the order to stand down, and President Ferdinand Marcos pardoned him. The heroic image often omits that his group allegedly killed up to about 30 islanders. Nor was he the last holdout: Teruo Nakamura was found on Morotai in December 1974.

John "Mad Jack" Churchill (1906 to 1996), a British officer, went through the Second World War with a longbow, a Scottish broadsword and bagpipes; he had competed for Britain at the 1939 world archery championships. As second in command of No. 3 Commando in the Vågsøy raid in Norway in December 1941, he reportedly played "The March of the Cameron Men" as the landing craft went in. In Italy in 1943, near the Salerno beachhead, he and a corporal took a German position and about 42 prisoners, earning him the Distinguished Service Order. Captured in Yugoslavia in 1944, he was held at Sachsenhausen and elsewhere. The most quoted story, that he killed a German soldier with an arrow in France in 1940, is widely repeated but thinly documented.

concepts.title: Phineas Gage: The Story That Grew
concepts.contentHtml:
On 13 September 1848, near Cavendish, Vermont, railroad construction foreman Phineas Gage was tamping blasting powder when it exploded. His tamping iron, a smooth rod about 3 feet 7 inches (1.1 m) long, 1.25 inches (3 cm) across and weighing 13.25 pounds (6 kg), passed up through his left cheek, behind the eye and out the top of his skull. He spoke within minutes. The local physician, John Martyn Harlow, controlled a dangerous infection, and Gage survived with much of his left frontal lobe destroyed.

The textbook version says he became a permanently impulsive, profane drifter, proof that personality lives in the frontal lobes. Its core is Harlow's 1868 report, written after Gage's death, saying friends found him "no longer Gage". Later writers added details with no source: that he became a violent drunk, abused a wife and children he never had, never held a job again, or died a sideshow attraction.

The psychologist Malcolm Macmillan, in An Odd Kind of Fame (2000), gathered the actual evidence. After a spell exhibiting himself, including, Harlow says, at Barnum's American Museum in New York, Gage worked about 18 months at a livery stable in Hanover, New Hampshire. From 1852 he drove stagecoaches on the Valparaíso to Santiago route in Chile for about seven years, demanding work that required planning, skill with horses and dealing with passengers. Macmillan argues this shows substantial social recovery, perhaps aided by the job's structured routine. Gage died near San Francisco in May 1860 after epileptic seizures. His skull and iron are in Harvard's Warren Anatomical Museum, and a portrait identified in 2009 shows a well-dressed, confident man holding the iron.

title: Hoaxes and Forgeries
description: A forged imperial decree, fake fossils, a stone giant, paper fairies and Hitler's diaries, and the methods that exposed them

concepts.title: The Donation of Constantine and Lorenzo Valla
concepts.contentHtml:
The Donation of Constantine presents itself as a decree of the emperor Constantine I. Cured of leprosy and baptized by Pope Sylvester I, Constantine grants the pope and his successors the Lateran Palace, imperial insignia, supremacy over the other great sees, and authority over Rome, Italy and the western provinces. It was forged, most likely in the 8th century, though some scholars argue for the 9th, and it entered medieval canon law collections, where popes and their critics argued over it for centuries.

Doubts were old: Otto III's chancery rejected it around 1001, and Nicholas of Cusa called it apocryphal in the 1430s. The humanist Lorenzo Valla attacked it in 1440, while he served Alfonso of Aragon, king of Naples, who was then in conflict with Pope Eugenius IV. Valla's weapon was philology. He showed that the Latin was not that of Constantine's age and used later terms, such as feudal vocabulary and "satraps" for Roman officials. He noted that it named Constantinople among the leading sees of the church when, at the document's supposed date, the city had not yet been founded. And he pointed out that no reliable earlier source mentioned so vast a gift.

Valla's treatise circulated in manuscript and was printed in the early 16th century by the German humanist Ulrich von Hutten; Martin Luther read it in 1520, and it hardened his hostility to the papacy. Its method, testing a text's language and claims against what is known of its supposed date, became a foundation of modern source criticism. The same logic, applied with chemistry and microscopes instead of grammar, exposed the later forgeries in this lesson.

concepts.title: Piltdown Man and the Cardiff Giant
concepts.contentHtml:
In December 1912 the amateur collector Charles Dawson and Arthur Smith Woodward of the British Museum (Natural History) announced skull fragments and a jaw from a gravel pit at Piltdown in Sussex. "Piltdown Man", named Eoanthropus dawsoni, combined a large, humanlike braincase with an apelike jaw, matching many scientists' expectation that a big brain came first. It also gave Britain a prestigious early human. As real fossils from Africa and Asia accumulated, Piltdown fit them less and less.

In 1953 Kenneth Oakley, Joseph Weiner and Wilfrid Le Gros Clark exposed it. Fluorine absorption tests showed the bones were far younger than claimed; the teeth showed file marks where they had been ground flat to look human; and the pieces had been stained with iron and chromic acid to look ancient. The jaw came from an orangutan and the skull from a modern human. A 2016 study using DNA and CT scans found the same orangutan's teeth at two Piltdown sites and one consistent forging technique, pointing to a single hoaxer, most likely Dawson.

The Cardiff Giant was cruder. George Hull, a New York tobacconist irritated by a revivalist's insistence on the literal giants of Genesis 6:4, had a ten-foot man carved from Iowa gypsum in Chicago and buried it on his cousin William Newell's farm at Cardiff, New York. Well diggers "found" it on 16 October 1869, and crowds paid 50 cents to look. The Yale paleontologist Othniel C. Marsh called it "a most decided humbug", noting fresh tool marks on soluble gypsum. Hull confessed that December. Refused the original, P. T. Barnum showed a copy. The line "There's a sucker born every minute" is pinned on Barnum without evidence; newspapers credited it to David Hannum, one of the giant's owners.

concepts.title: Paper Fairies and Fake Diaries
concepts.contentHtml:
In 1917 in Cottingley, near Bradford, 16-year-old Elsie Wright and her 9-year-old cousin Frances Griffiths photographed each other with what looked like dancing fairies and a gnome; three more photographs followed in 1920. The Theosophist Edward Gardner promoted them, a photography expert found no double exposure, and Kodak declined to certify them. Sir Arthur Conan Doyle published them in The Strand Magazine in December 1920 and wrote The Coming of the Fairies (1922). The fairies were paper cutouts Elsie had copied from Princess Mary's Gift Book (1914), with wings added, held up with hatpins. After an investigation by the photographic editor Geoffrey Crawley, both women admitted the fakes in 1983, though Frances insisted the fifth photograph was genuine.

In April 1983 the West German magazine Stern announced 60 volumes of Hitler's diaries, bought through its reporter Gerd Heidemann for 9.3 million Deutsche Marks. The historian Hugh Trevor-Roper vouched for them, then voiced doubts at the press conference. Tests organized by the Federal Archives settled the matter within two weeks: the paper glowed under ultraviolet light with a brightener absent from wartime paper, the bindings contained polyester made after 1953, and ink tests suggested recent writing. Much of the text was copied, errors and all, from a published collection of Hitler's speeches. On 6 May 1983 the government declared the diaries fakes.

The forger, Konrad Kujau, had even put the initials "FH" instead of "AH" on a cover, using plastic letters from a department store. In 1985 he and Heidemann were each jailed for more than four years. As with Piltdown, the experts' desire for the find did as much work as the forger's skill.

title: Strange Trials and Stranger Afterlives
description: A dead pope in the dock, pigs on the gallows, a wandering head, a philosopher on display and a library saved by fire

concepts.title: Corpses on Trial: Formosus and Cromwell
concepts.contentHtml:
In January 897 CE Pope Stephen VI had the corpse of Pope Formosus, dead for about nine months, dug up, dressed in papal vestments and seated on a throne in the Lateran basilica in Rome to stand trial. A deacon answered for the dead man. The charges were canonical: that Formosus had moved from the see of Porto to Rome against church law, had committed perjury, and had acted as a bishop while reduced to lay status. He was convicted, stripped of his vestments and of the three fingers of his right hand used in blessing, and his acts and ordinations were annulled. His body was thrown into the Tiber.

The quarrel was political. Formosus had crowned the East Frankish king Arnulf of Carinthia emperor in 896, against the rival house of Spoleto. Older accounts blame Lambert of Spoleto and his mother Ageltrude for the trial; other historians note that Lambert later approved its annulment and look to other Spoletan or Roman factions. The backlash was quick. Stephen was deposed and strangled in prison that summer; in December 897 Pope Theodore II reburied Formosus in St Peter's, and John IX banned trials of the dead in 898. The main narrative source, Liutprand of Cremona, wrote decades later, so its vivid details need some caution.

England staged its own posthumous punishment. Oliver Cromwell died in September 1658 and was buried in Westminster Abbey. After the restoration of Charles II, Parliament ordered the bodies of Cromwell, his son-in-law Henry Ireton and the regicide judge John Bradshaw dug up. On 30 January 1661, twelve years to the day after Charles I's execution, the corpses were hanged at Tyburn, then beheaded, and the heads were set on poles above Westminster Hall.

concepts.title: Animals in the Dock
concepts.contentHtml:
From the 13th to the 18th centuries, European courts, especially in France, sometimes prosecuted animals. Two kinds of case appear. Secular courts tried individual domestic animals, most often pigs, which roamed freely in towns, for killing or injuring people, frequently infants. Church courts proceeded against whole populations of pests, such as rats, weevils and caterpillars, which could be summoned, given appointed lawyers and threatened with anathema.

The best-known secular case is the sow of Falaise in Normandy, executed in 1386 after the death of a child. The firm evidence is an executioner's receipt dated 9 January 1386, recording payment for dragging and hanging a sow of about three years that had eaten a child's face, plus the cost of a new glove. Later accounts add that the sow was maimed to match the child's wounds, dressed in human clothes and hanged before a crowd, and that a church mural showed the scene until it was whitewashed in the 19th century. Those details come from much later writers and deserve caution.

The classic collection, E. P. Evans's The Criminal Prosecution and Capital Punishment of Animals (1906), is valuable but uncritical. Explanations differ. Some historians see the trials as rituals that restored an order broken by a killing; others stress ordinary legal procedure applied to dangerous property; the economist Peter Leeson has argued that church trials of pests encouraged tithe payment. In a case recorded at Saint-Julien in Savoy, weevils in the vineyards were prosecuted in 1545 and again from 1587, and at one stage the townspeople offered the insects a plot of land of their own.

concepts.title: Stranger Afterlives: A Head, a Philosopher and a Library
concepts.contentHtml:
Cromwell's head stayed above Westminster Hall into the 1680s. Tradition says a storm brought it down and a sentry took it home, but its whereabouts from about 1684 to 1710 are unknown. After passing through several collectors and showmen, it was bought by the Wilkinson family in 1815. A 1934 study by Karl Pearson and Geoffrey Morant judged it genuine with "moral certainty". On 25 March 1960 it was buried at Sidney Sussex College, Cambridge, Cromwell's old college, in a spot that remains undisclosed.

The philosopher Jeremy Bentham, who died on 6 June 1832, wanted his body to be useful. Following his instructions, the physician Thomas Southwood Smith dissected it publicly as an anatomy lecture, then assembled the skeleton, dressed in Bentham's clothes, in a cabinet: the "auto-icon". The attempt to mummify the head left it dark and shrunken, so a wax head was fitted. The auto-icon reached University College London in 1850; the real head, a favorite target of student pranks, is locked away. Bentham did not found UCL, though he is called its spiritual father, and he does not routinely attend council meetings "present but not voting"; he was wheeled into one in 2013.

The library of the Assyrian king Ashurbanipal (reigned 669 to c. 631 BCE) survived because it was destroyed. When Babylonians, Medes and their allies sacked Nineveh in 612 BCE, the burning palaces are thought to have partly baked many unfired clay tablets, hardening them under the rubble. Excavations led by Austen Henry Layard and Hormuzd Rassam from 1849 recovered more than 30,000 tablets and fragments, now in the British Museum, including omens, letters, scholarly texts and the Epic of Gilgamesh, whose flood story George Smith announced in 1872. Findspots went largely unrecorded, so the library's original layout is hard to reconstruct.
